entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A typical feature that clearly identifies a person, style, type of thing or condition.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, reviews and educated speech, usually as *a hallmark of* or *the hallmark of* + a person, style, era or condition. It is often praise (*attention to detail is the hallmark of her work*), but it also works for neutral or negative signs, as in *the hallmarks of cancer*. *Have all the hallmarks of* means to look exactly like a typical case.
entries.pattern: a / the hallmark of something; have / bear all the hallmarks of something
examples: Short, punchy sentences are a **hallmark** of her writing; you can recognize her columns without seeing the name.
The robbery had all the **hallmarks** of an inside job: no forced entry and the alarm switched off.
Extreme tiredness after even light exercise is a **hallmark** of chronic fatigue syndrome.

drill.sentence: The movie has all the {{hallmarks}} of a summer blockbuster: car chases, explosions and a one-liner in every scene.
drill.hint: typical identifying features (not *signs*, *trappings* or *makings*)

entries.related: *trademark* — a feature closely linked to one person, often informal (*his trademark grin*); *characteristic* — plainer, more neutral; *sign* — any indication.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Clearly and without doubt; it stresses that a quality is definite, not slight.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, reviews and educated speech before adjectives and comparatives: *decidedly mixed*, *decidedly better*, *decidedly unimpressed*. It often adds a dry, slightly ironic tone, especially before negative words (*a decidedly unglamorous job*). For acting with firm, quick decisions, use *decisively* instead.
entries.pattern: decidedly + adjective / comparative (decidedly mixed / better / unimpressed)
examples: The hotel looked lovely online, but in person it was **decidedly** shabby.
After three days of rain, the campers were looking **decidedly** less cheerful.
The new version of the app is **decidedly** faster, though it still crashes now and then.

drill.sentence: Opinions on the new office layout are {{decidedly}} mixed: some people love the open space, others miss their doors.
drill.hint: clearly, without any doubt (not *distinctly*)

entries.related: *distinctly* — very close (*distinctly uncomfortable*); *definitely* — more common in speech, about certainty rather than degree; *decisively* — in a firm, determined way.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In a way that is widely known, usually because something is bad, difficult or unreliable.
entries.usage: Very common in journalism and conversation before adjectives: *notoriously difficult*, *notoriously unreliable*, *notoriously hard to predict*. It implies a well-known bad reputation, so it is often used humorously about everyday things (*notoriously slow Wi-Fi*). For a good reputation, use *famously* instead.
entries.pattern: notoriously + difficult / hard / unreliable / slow / expensive
examples: San Francisco is **notoriously** expensive; rent for a one-bedroom can be more than a mortgage payment elsewhere.
My dad is **notoriously** bad at keeping secrets, so don't tell him about the party.
Fine-tuning very large networks is **notoriously** sensitive to the learning rate.

drill.sentence: Cats are {{notoriously}} hard to train, so don't expect her to come when you call.
drill.hint: as everyone knows, in a bad way (not *famously*)

entries.related: *famously* — well known, often in a good or neutral way; *infamously* — known for something shameful, stronger; *notably* — in a way worth noticing.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Fair and reasonable to everyone involved, especially in how money, work or resources are shared.
entries.usage: Used in legal, business, policy and academic writing: *an equitable solution*, *equitable distribution*, *equitable access to* healthcare or education. In conversation, *fair* is far more natural, and *equitable* can sound like official language. It does not have to mean *equal*: an equitable split may give people different amounts.
entries.pattern: an equitable solution / share / split / distribution; equitable access to something
examples: Under **equitable** distribution, a divorce court splits property fairly, which doesn't always mean fifty-fifty.
A more **equitable** way to split rent is to pay in proportion to the size of each bedroom.
The school district wants more **equitable** access to advanced math classes across all its high schools.

drill.sentence: With the lawyer's help, my parents worked out an {{equitable}} split: my brother gets the farm, and I get the house and the savings.
drill.hint: just and reasonable, though not equal (formal; not *fair* or *even*)

entries.related: *fair* — the everyday word; *equal* — exactly the same for everyone; *even-handed* — treating all sides the same, often about judges or reporting.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To consider or officially judge something to be a certain way.
entries.usage: Typical of legal, official and news language, very often in the passive: *was deemed unsafe*, *deemed necessary*, *deemed fit to stand trial*. The adjective or noun follows directly (*deem something appropriate*), sometimes with *to be*. In casual speech it sounds stiff or jokingly pompous; people say *think* or *consider*.
entries.pattern: be deemed (to be) + adjective / noun; deem something necessary / appropriate
examples: After the earthquake, half the buildings on the block were **deemed** unsafe to enter.
The referee **deemed** the tackle dangerous and showed a red card.
You can bring one carry-on bag, plus any medical equipment your doctor **deems** necessary.

drill.sentence: The old pier was {{deemed}} too dangerous for the public and closed for repairs.
drill.hint: formally regarded as being (not *considered* or *declared*)

mistake.wrong: The bridge was deemed as unsafe.
mistake.why: *Deem* takes the adjective or noun directly; *deemed as* does occur in native writing, but style guides and editors mark it as an error.

entries.related: *consider* — the everyday equivalent; *judge* — stresses a decision after thought; *regard as* — needs *as*.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: So unreasonable or silly that it is ridiculous and impossible to take seriously.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, opinion writing and reviews to dismiss an idea, price or claim with scorn: *a ludicrous suggestion*, *ludicrous prices*. It is a little stronger and more educated-sounding than *ridiculous*, and *absolutely ludicrous* is a frequent combination. A typical pattern is *it's ludicrous to think that…*.
entries.pattern: absolutely / utterly ludicrous; it's ludicrous to + verb / that …
examples: Twelve dollars for a small coffee? That's absolutely **ludicrous**.
The movie's plot gets more **ludicrous** by the minute, but the action scenes are fun.
It's **ludicrous** to expect new hires to learn the whole system in their first week.

drill.sentence: The landlord tried to charge us a fee for returning our own keys, which was frankly {{ludicrous}}.
drill.hint: so unreasonable it's impossible to take seriously (not *ridiculous*, *absurd* or *preposterous*)

entries.related: *ridiculous* — the everyday word, slightly weaker; *absurd* — illogical, also used in philosophy; *preposterous* — very close, a bit more formal.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very ambitious, noble or idealistic, often more than seems realistic.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and business writing with *goals*, *ambitions*, *ideals*, *expectations* and *promises*. It is often slightly skeptical: *lofty goals* suggests they may be hard to reach. The literal sense, very high, appears mostly in literary writing and real-estate ads (*lofty ceilings*).
entries.pattern: lofty goals / ambitions / ideals / expectations / promises
examples: The startup has **lofty** ambitions: it wants to replace every bank card in the country within five years.
We started January with **lofty** goals, like running a marathon, and ended it walking the dog.
Fans had **lofty** expectations for the sequel, and most of them left the theater disappointed.

drill.sentence: The team set itself the {{lofty}} goal of winning the championship, even though they'd finished last the year before.
drill.hint: very high-minded and hard to reach (not *ambitious*)

entries.related: *ambitious* — neutral, often positive; *grandiose* — impressive-sounding but unrealistic, critical; *noble* — morally admirable.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To mention a law, rule, principle or authority as support or justification for what you say or do.
entries.usage: Common in legal, political and academic writing: *invoke the Fifth Amendment*, *invoke a clause*, *invoke someone's name*. It often suggests that the reference is used strategically, sometimes as an excuse. In programming it also means to call a function, which is a separate, technical sense.
entries.pattern: invoke a law / clause / right / principle; invoke someone's name
examples: The witness **invoked** her right to remain silent and refused to answer.
The new coach often **invokes** the legendary teams of the 1980s to motivate his players.
My little brother **invokes** the five-second rule every time he drops a cookie on the floor.

drill.sentence: The neighbors {{invoked}} the city's noise ordinance to stop the late-night parties next door.
drill.hint: appealed to (a rule) as support (not *cited*)

mistake.wrong: The smell of pine invokes memories of my childhood.
mistake.right: The smell of pine evokes memories of my childhood.
mistake.why: *Evoke* brings feelings or memories to mind; *invoke* means appealing to a rule, authority or principle.

entries.related: *cite* — mention as evidence, more neutral; *appeal to* — very close, often for principles or emotions; *evoke* — call up a feeling or image.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Dealing with something as a whole system and considering how its parts affect each other, rather than looking at single parts.
entries.usage: Very common in education, healthcare, management and HR language: *a holistic approach*, *a holistic view*, *holistic admissions*. It can sound like a buzzword, and in medicine it may suggest alternative therapies, so precise writers sometimes prefer *comprehensive* or *integrated*. It usually comes before a noun.
entries.pattern: a holistic approach / view / review / assessment (of / to something)
examples: Our gardener takes a **holistic** approach: instead of spraying the pests, she improves the soil and plants flowers that attract ladybugs.
Good financial planners take a **holistic** view of your money, from debt and savings to retirement.
Instead of tuning each microservice separately, we need a **holistic** view of the whole system's latency.

drill.sentence: The coach's {{holistic}} approach to training covers sleep, nutrition and mental health, not just practice.
drill.hint: looking at the whole person rather than separate parts (not *comprehensive*)

entries.related: *comprehensive* — covering everything, but not about interactions; *integrated* — with parts combined into one system; *piecemeal* — the opposite, done in separate bits.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very skilled at something, especially something that needs quickness or cleverness.
entries.usage: Used in writing and educated speech, nearly always with *at* (*adept at handling difficult customers*), sometimes with *in* or *with*. It often describes social or practical skills and can be ironic (*adept at dodging work*). It is more formal than *good at* and suggests ease and quickness.
entries.pattern: adept at + noun / -ing; adept with tools / words
examples: Toddlers are remarkably **adept** at finding the one thing you don't want them to touch.
She's **adept** at calming angry customers without promising anything she can't deliver.
Scammers have become **adept** at copying bank websites down to the last detail.

drill.sentence: My grandmother is surprisingly {{adept}} at video calls; she even uses filters to make us laugh.
drill.hint: highly capable and quick (not *good* or *skilled*)

entries.related: *skilled* — trained and capable, more neutral; *deft* — skillful in a quick, light way, often with the hands; *inept* — the opposite, clumsy and incompetent.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: In perfect condition, as if new or untouched; also completely clean.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, ads and travel writing: *pristine condition*, *pristine beaches*, *pristine wilderness*. In listings for cars, books or sneakers, *in pristine condition* means like new; for nature it means untouched by people. Americans say both PRIS-teen and pris-TEEN.
entries.pattern: in pristine condition; pristine beaches / snow / wilderness
examples: I'm selling my old guitar; it's twenty years old but in **pristine** condition.
The island's **pristine** beaches attract divers from all over the world.
We woke up to **pristine** snow covering the whole yard, until the dog ran through it.

drill.sentence: He keeps his vintage Mustang in {{pristine}} condition and won't even let us eat near it.
drill.hint: as good as new, with no wear at all (not *mint*, *perfect* or *immaculate*)

entries.related: *immaculate* — perfectly clean and tidy; *mint* — informal, in *mint condition*, like new; *spotless* — completely clean; *unspoiled* — about places untouched by development.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A feeling that someone or something is not good enough to deserve your respect or attention.
entries.usage: Used in writing and educated speech, often with *for*: *disdain for authority*, *with open disdain*, *a look of disdain*. It describes a cold, superior attitude rather than hot anger. It is also a verb (*she disdains small talk*), which sounds more literary.
entries.pattern: disdain for someone / something; with (open) disdain; a look of disdain
examples: My teenage son watches my dance moves with pure **disdain**.
The chef makes no secret of his **disdain** for ketchup.
The critic's review of the remake dripped with **disdain**.

drill.sentence: She has nothing but {{disdain}} for people who leave their shopping carts in the middle of the parking lot.
drill.hint: the cold feeling that something isn't worth respecting (not *contempt* or *scorn*)

entries.related: *contempt* — stronger, often mixed with anger; *scorn* — open, mocking disdain; *indifference* — not caring at all.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To push someone out of a central or influential role, so that they have little say in what happens.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and sports writing, very often in the passive: *was sidelined*, *felt sidelined*. About people at work or in families, it suggests unfair or deliberate exclusion. In sports it also means kept out of games, usually by injury (*sidelined with a knee injury*).
entries.pattern: be / feel sidelined (by someone); sideline someone
examples: After the merger, the founder was quietly **sidelined** and left the company a year later.
Grandpa felt **sidelined** when his kids started planning the reunion without him.
Critics say the new rules **sideline** small farmers in favor of large agricultural companies.

drill.sentence: Once her younger brother took over the family bakery, she felt completely {{sidelined}}, and nobody asked her opinion anymore.
drill.hint: pushed out of an important role (not *excluded* or *marginalized*)

entries.related: *marginalize* — push a person or group to the edge of society or power, more formal; *push aside* — informal; *bench* — in sports and informally, take someone out of play.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To enjoy something very much, or to look forward to it with pleasure.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and conversation: *relish the chance*, *relish a challenge*, *relish the role of…*. It is very frequent in negatives for things you dread: *I don't relish the idea of telling her*. It takes a noun or an *-ing* form.
entries.pattern: relish + the chance / challenge / -ing; not relish the thought / idea of something
examples: She's the kind of lawyer who **relishes** a tough cross-examination.
I don't **relish** the thought of driving six hours with two kids in the back seat.
The underdogs **relished** the chance to knock the champions out of the tournament.

drill.sentence: Nobody {{relishes}} the job of cleaning out the fridge after a two-week vacation.
drill.hint: takes great pleasure in (not *enjoys* or *loves*)

mistake.wrong: She relishes to argue with her brother.
mistake.right: She relishes arguing with her brother.
mistake.why: Like *enjoy*, *relish* is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form, not by *to* + verb.

entries.related: *savor* — enjoy slowly, often food or a moment; *look forward to* — neutral, no strong pleasure; *dread* — the opposite. The noun *relish* is also the chopped-pickle topping on hot dogs.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The typical spirit, values and attitudes of a group, organization or period.
entries.usage: Common in business, education and cultural writing: *the company's ethos*, *a team ethos*, *the ethos of the 1960s*. It sounds more formal and thoughtful than *culture* or *values*, and in casual speech it can sound like corporate language. Typical partners are *strong*, *shared*, *founding* and *public-service*.
entries.pattern: the ethos of + group / era; a company / team / public-service ethos
examples: The bakery's **ethos** is simple: everything is made from scratch, every morning.
The open-source **ethos** of sharing code freely has shaped how scientists work.
The team's **ethos** of hard work and humility came straight from their old coach.

drill.sentence: The summer camp's {{ethos}} of kindness and inclusion shapes everything, from cabin assignments to the evening games.
drill.hint: the shared values that define a group (not *culture*, *spirit* or *ethic*)

entries.related: *culture* — broader, includes habits and practices; *values* — the beliefs themselves; *zeitgeist* — the spirit of a whole period, more literary.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Done or shown openly, so that it can be seen, not hidden or secret.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, law and academic writing, often in contrast with *covert* or *subtle*: *overt hostility*, *overt discrimination*, *overt threats*. It is usually about negative behavior and stresses that nothing is hidden; in conversation, *open* or *obvious* is more natural. Americans stress it either way: oh-VURT or OH-vurt.
entries.pattern: overt hostility / criticism / discrimination / threats; overt rather than subtle
examples: There was no **overt** hostility at dinner, but the tension between my aunts was obvious.
The ad avoids any **overt** sales pitch; it just shows people enjoying the product.
Discrimination at work is often subtle rather than **overt**, which makes it harder to prove.

drill.sentence: Teachers can deal with {{overt}} bullying like shoving and name-calling; it's the covert kind in group chats that's harder to catch.
drill.hint: done openly, where everyone can see it (not *open* or *obvious*)

entries.related: *covert* — the opposite, secret; *blatant* — very obvious and shameless; *explicit* — clearly stated in words.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Too pleased with yourself and your own cleverness or luck, in a way that annoys other people.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and reviews, and always critical: *a smug grin*, *a smug look*, *don't be so smug*. It describes someone who shows satisfaction about being right or better off than others. *Self-satisfied* is close and more formal; the noun is *smugness*.
entries.pattern: a smug smile / grin / look / tone; smug about something
examples: He gave me a **smug** little smile when the GPS proved his route was faster.
Don't get too **smug**; you only won because the other team had three injured players.
The ad's **smug** tone, which implied everyone else was doing it wrong, annoyed a lot of viewers.

drill.sentence: After she correctly guessed the ending of the movie, my sister was unbearably {{smug}} for the rest of the night.
drill.hint: showing annoying satisfaction with herself (not *proud* or *cocky*)

entries.related: *self-satisfied* — very close, more formal; *cocky* — informal, too confident; *complacent* — so satisfied that you stop trying.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A return of activity, interest or strength after a period of decline.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and cultural writing: *a resurgence of interest in vinyl*, *a resurgence in bedbug cases*. It can describe good or bad things and is usually followed by *of* or *in*. Typical partners are *enjoy* or *see a resurgence*, and adjectives such as *recent*, *strong* and *unexpected*.
entries.pattern: a resurgence of / in + something; enjoy / see a resurgence
examples: Vinyl records have enjoyed a remarkable **resurgence**, and our local record store is busy again.
Hotels in several cities have reported a **resurgence** of bedbugs this summer.
Neural networks were out of fashion in the early 2000s, before their dramatic **resurgence** around 2012.

drill.sentence: Board games are having a real {{resurgence}}: the coffee shop in my neighborhood now hosts game nights twice a week.
drill.hint: return to popularity after a decline (not *revival*, *renaissance* or *comeback*)

entries.related: *revival* — very close, often about art, music or an old show; *comeback* — informal, often about people; *decline* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Happening only now and then, at irregular times or in scattered places, not continuously.
entries.usage: Common in news and reports: *sporadic fighting*, *sporadic showers*, *sporadic outages*. It stresses that events are scattered and unpredictable, not regular. The adverb *sporadically* is just as common (*the bus runs sporadically on weekends*).
entries.pattern: sporadic showers / outages / fighting / attempts; only sporadic
examples: The forecast calls for **sporadic** showers, so I'd bring an umbrella just in case.
My attempts to learn the guitar have been **sporadic** at best, mostly around New Year's.
Users reported **sporadic** outages all morning, but the company says the service is stable now.

drill.sentence: My brother's emails are {{sporadic}}: nothing for months, then five in one day.
drill.hint: arriving now and then with no pattern (not *irregular* or *occasional*)

entries.related: *intermittent* — stopping and starting, often about rain, pain or signals; *occasional* — now and then, more neutral; *constant* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A possible way of getting help or compensation when you are in a difficult situation, especially through an official or legal process.
entries.usage: Typical of legal, consumer and financial writing, very often in negatives and questions: *have no recourse*, *What recourse do I have?*, *legal recourse*. The more formal *have recourse to* + something means to use it as a way out. Americans say both REE-korss and rih-KORSS.
entries.pattern: have no / little recourse; legal recourse; recourse against someone; have recourse to something
examples: If the airline loses your bag, what **recourse** do you actually have?
Because she'd signed the contract, she had little **recourse** when the gym kept charging her.
Tenants have legal **recourse** if a landlord refuses to return their deposit.

drill.sentence: The seller disappeared after we paid, and since we'd used cash, we had no {{recourse}}.
drill.hint: official way to get help or our money back (not *options* or *remedy*)

entries.related: *remedy* — legal term for a solution or compensation; *redress* — formal, putting a wrong right; *resource* — a supply of something useful, a different word.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In a clear and noticeable way; it shows that a difference or change is large enough to see easily.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and academic writing with comparisons and verbs of change: *markedly different*, *markedly better*, *improve markedly*, *differ markedly*. It sounds more formal than *noticeably* or *a lot*. It has three syllables: the *-ed* is pronounced.
entries.pattern: markedly different / better / higher; differ / improve / increase markedly
examples: Her mood has improved **markedly** since she started sleeping eight hours a night.
The two brothers have **markedly** different ideas about how to run the family farm.
Error rates were **markedly** lower when the radiologists used the AI tool.

drill.sentence: Prices at the farmers' market are {{markedly}} higher this year, thanks to the drought.
drill.hint: to a visible, striking degree, in formal style (not *much*, *noticeably* or *significantly*)

mistake.why: In *markedly*, as in *supposedly* and *allegedly*, the *-ed* before *-ly* is a full syllable.

entries.related: *noticeably* — a bit less formal; *significantly* — in research, implies statistical significance; *substantially* — by a large amount.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Completely determined and refusing to change your opinion or decision, however much others try to persuade you.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation, especially when reporting what someone insists on: *She was adamant that she never got the email*. It usually comes after *be* or *remain* and is followed by a *that*-clause or *about*. It suggests strong emotion as well as firmness.
entries.pattern: be / remain adamant that …; adamant about something
examples: My dad is **adamant** that he doesn't need a hearing aid, even though he can't hear the doorbell.
The coach remained **adamant** that the goal should have counted.
Despite the recall, the company is **adamant** that its products are safe.

drill.sentence: I suggested we skip the wedding, but my wife was {{adamant}}: we're going, and we're staying until the end.
drill.hint: absolutely unwilling to change her mind (not *firm* or *insistent*)

entries.related: *insistent* — repeatedly demanding; *firm* — calmer, less emotional; *unyielding* — formal; *flexible* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The basic principles, facts or things on which something else depends.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, speeches and business writing: *the bedrock of democracy*, *trust is the bedrock of any relationship*. It suggests something solid and lasting, so it often comes in praise or warnings. It is also used before nouns: *bedrock values*, *a bedrock principle*.
entries.pattern: the bedrock of something; bedrock principles / values / beliefs
examples: Trust is the **bedrock** of any good marriage.
Small family farms were once the **bedrock** of the local economy.
Reproducibility is a **bedrock** principle of science, yet few studies are ever repeated.

drill.sentence: The public library has been the {{bedrock}} of this town's community life for over a century.
drill.hint: the solid base everything rests on (not *heart*, *foundation* or *cornerstone*)

entries.related: *cornerstone* — one key part that supports the rest; *foundation* — more neutral; *backbone* — the main source of strength.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Comfort or relief that makes a sad or difficult situation easier to bear.
entries.usage: Used in writing and thoughtful speech, especially about grief and hard times: *find solace in music*, *take solace in the fact that…*, *seek solace*. It is usually uncountable (*find solace*, not *find a solace*). It sounds warmer and more literary than *comfort*.
entries.pattern: find / take solace in something; seek solace; a source of solace
examples: The insurance check offered little **solace** to families who had lost irreplaceable photos in the fire.
We lost the final, but we can take **solace** in the fact that nobody expected us to get that far.
In the months after the layoffs, he sought **solace** in woodworking and cooking.

drill.sentence: When her cat died, she took some {{solace}} in knowing that it had lived a long, happy life.
drill.hint: emotional relief in a sad time (not *comfort* or *consolation*)

mistake.why: The stress is on the first syllable, and the second vowel is a weak schwa, not *lace*.

entries.related: *comfort* — the everyday word; *consolation* — something that makes a loss feel less bad, often *some consolation*; *despair* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not secure or stable, and likely to fall, fail or get worse at any moment.
entries.usage: Common in news and serious writing about jobs, money, health and housing: *a precarious position*, *precarious finances*, *precarious work*. It is also used literally for things that might fall (*a precarious stack of plates*). It is stronger than *uncertain*: it suggests real danger.
entries.pattern: a precarious position / situation / balance; precarious finances / work
examples: A **precarious** tower of dirty dishes was balanced on the edge of the sink.
Many gig workers live in a **precarious** situation, with no sick pay and no guaranteed hours.
The team is in a **precarious** position: one more loss and they're out of the playoffs.

drill.sentence: With two kids, no savings and a car that keeps breaking down, their finances are pretty {{precarious}}.
drill.hint: at risk of falling apart at any moment (not *shaky* or *fragile*)

entries.related: *unstable* — more general; *shaky* — informal, weak or uncertain; *perilous* — full of serious danger, more literary; *secure* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Causing a strong feeling of sadness, regret or tenderness, often in a quiet, touching way.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, journalism and thoughtful conversation about moments, scenes, memories and reminders: *a poignant moment*, *a poignant reminder of…*. It describes the thing that moves you, not the person who feels it; that person feels *moved*. The *g* is silent.
entries.pattern: a poignant moment / scene / reminder / letter; a poignant reminder of something
examples: The most **poignant** moment of the wedding was when the bride danced with her grandfather.
The empty chair at the table was a **poignant** reminder that Dad wasn't with us this Thanksgiving.
The film ends with a quiet, **poignant** scene between two old friends who never made up.

drill.sentence: Finding my late mother's handwritten recipe cards was both lovely and deeply {{poignant}}.
drill.hint: sad in a tender, heart-tugging way (not *moving*, *touching* or *painful*)

mistake.why: The *g* is silent; *gn* here sounds like the *ny* in *canyon*.

entries.related: *moving* — causing strong emotion, sad or happy; *touching* — gently moving, often about kindness; *bittersweet* — both happy and sad.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something that encourages a process or activity to start or to happen faster.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and academic writing: *the impetus for the change*, *give new impetus to*, *provide the impetus*. It often comes with *new*, *fresh*, *added* or *the main*, and is followed by *for* or *to*. Stress the first syllable: IM-puh-tus.
entries.pattern: the impetus for something; give / provide (new) impetus to something
examples: A scary checkup at the dentist was the **impetus** I needed to finally quit soda.
The flood gave new **impetus** to plans for a sea wall around the harbor.
The main **impetus** for the change came from a nurse who was tired of paper forms.

drill.sentence: Their first grandchild was the {{impetus}} for my parents to finally sell the house and move closer to us.
drill.hint: what finally pushed them to act (not *motivation*, *catalyst* or *incentive*)

entries.related: *catalyst* — something that causes a quick change; *momentum* — the force of something already moving; *incentive* — a reward that motivates.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make it harder for someone or something to move, act or make progress.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and business writing, often in the passive: *hampered by injuries*, *hampered by bad weather*, *hampered by a lack of funding*. It describes an obstacle that slows things down rather than stopping them completely. The noun *hamper* is a different word: a large basket, in American English usually for dirty laundry.
entries.pattern: be hampered by + bad weather / injuries / a lack of something; hamper efforts / progress
examples: Rescue efforts were **hampered** by heavy snow and fallen power lines.
The team's season was **hampered** by injuries to its two best players.
Constant interruptions **hamper** my ability to focus when I work from home.

drill.sentence: Poor cell service {{hampered}} our efforts to find each other at the music festival.
drill.hint: made harder and slower (not *hindered* or *complicated*)

entries.related: *hinder* — very close, a bit more formal; *impede* — formal, often about movement or progress; *hold back* — informal.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Lasting much longer than expected or than is usual, often in a tiring or unpleasant way.
entries.usage: Typical of news, legal and business writing: *protracted negotiations*, *a protracted legal battle*, *a protracted illness*. It usually comes before a noun and sounds critical or weary. In conversation, *drawn-out* or *long* is more natural.
entries.pattern: protracted negotiations / dispute / legal battle / illness
examples: After a **protracted** legal battle, the family finally won the right to keep the house.
The strike ended after **protracted** negotiations over pay and health insurance.
Her recovery from the surgery was more **protracted** than the doctors had predicted.

drill.sentence: The divorce turned into a {{protracted}} fight over who would get the dog.
drill.hint: dragging on much longer than expected (not *lengthy*, *prolonged* or *drawn-out*)

entries.related: *lengthy* — long, more neutral; *drawn-out* — less formal; *prolonged* — very close, also common in medicine (*prolonged exposure*).

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A deep, often vague feeling of anxiety and worry, especially about yourself, your life or the world.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, journalism and reviews, often with a slightly humorous or critical tone: *teenage angst*, *existential angst*, *angst over* a decision. It is uncountable. Unlike German *Angst*, it does not mean ordinary fear of a danger; it suggests brooding, self-focused worry.
entries.pattern: teenage / existential angst; angst over / about something
examples: Her early songs are full of teenage **angst**: breakups, strict parents and feeling misunderstood.
There's a lot of **angst** in the office about the upcoming reorganization.
After weeks of **angst** over which college to choose, he finally flipped a coin.

drill.sentence: His diary from age fifteen is pure teenage {{angst}}: nobody understands him, and life is meaningless.
drill.hint: brooding worry about yourself and your life (not *drama* or *anxiety*)

entries.related: *anxiety* — the general and medical word; *dread* — fear of something specific in the future; *ennui* — boredom and dissatisfaction, more literary.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To understand something that seems very strange, hard to believe or hard to explain.
entries.usage: Used in conversation and writing almost only in negatives and questions: *I can't fathom why…*, *hard to fathom*, *impossible to fathom*. It usually expresses surprise or disbelief more than intellectual difficulty. As a noun, a *fathom* is a unit of water depth (six feet).
entries.pattern: can't fathom why / how / what …; hard / difficult to fathom
examples: I can't **fathom** why anyone would pay four hundred dollars for a pair of sneakers.
The scale of the damage after the hurricane was hard to **fathom**.
Investigators still can't **fathom** how a ship that size ran aground on a clear, calm night.

drill.sentence: My grandmother still can't {{fathom}} how people meet their partners on an app.
drill.hint: begin to understand, in a tone of disbelief (not *grasp* or *comprehend*)

entries.related: *comprehend* — formal, understand fully; *grasp* — understand an idea; *get your head around* — informal, manage to understand.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To express sadness, regret or disappointment about something, often something lost or something that has changed.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and literary writing, often to report complaints: *Fans lamented the loss of…*, *she lamented that…*. In conversation it can sound formal or mock-serious (*he lamented the closing of his favorite diner*). The noun *lament* is also used, as is the adjective *lamentable* (regrettably bad).
entries.pattern: lament the loss / decline / passing of something; lament that …
examples: Longtime residents **lament** the loss of the neighborhood's small shops to chain stores.
"Nobody writes real letters anymore," my grandmother **lamented** as she sorted the mail.
Teachers often **lament** that students no longer read whole books.

drill.sentence: Every time we drive past the old stadium site, my uncle {{laments}} that it's now a parking garage.
drill.hint: says sadly and regretfully (not *complains*)

entries.related: *mourn* — feel deep sadness, especially for a death; *bemoan* — complain about, a bit critical; *deplore* — strongly condemn.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To deliberately avoid someone or something, often because you disapprove of them or want to exclude them.
entries.usage: Used in journalism and serious writing, both for social exclusion (*shunned by the community*) and for rejecting things (*shun publicity*, *shun processed food*). It is often passive and sounds stronger and more deliberate than *avoid*. In casual speech, *avoid* or *steer clear of* is more natural.
entries.pattern: shun someone; be shunned by family / the community; shun publicity / the spotlight
examples: After he testified against his old friends, he was **shunned** by the whole neighborhood.
The author **shuns** publicity and has never given a TV interview.
Many young people now **shun** cable TV in favor of streaming.

drill.sentence: Despite her fame, the actress {{shuns}} social media and doesn't even own a smartphone.
drill.hint: deliberately rejects and stays away from (not *avoids*)

entries.related: *avoid* — neutral, the everyday word; *ostracize* — exclude someone from a group, formal; *spurn* — reject with contempt.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To choose not to demand a fee, a right or a rule, so that it does not apply in a particular case.
entries.usage: Common in business, legal and customer-service language: *waive a fee*, *waive the deposit*, *waive your right to a jury trial*. Customers often ask *Can you waive the fee?*, and companies say *the fee will be waived*. It sounds exactly like *wave*, and even native writers mix up the spelling.
entries.pattern: waive a fee / fine / requirement / right; the fee is waived
examples: The bank agreed to **waive** the late fee since it was my first time.
The defendant **waived** his right to a jury trial and let the judge decide the case.
The museum **waives** admission on the first Sunday of every month.

drill.sentence: If you sign up for a full year, the gym will {{waive}} the hundred-dollar enrollment fee.
drill.hint: choose not to charge, formal word (not *drop*)

entries.related: *forgo* — give up something you want; *exempt (from)* — free someone from a rule; *enforce* — the opposite, make a rule apply.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Spreading or causing harm slowly and quietly, so that the damage is not noticed until it is serious.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, medicine and serious writing about diseases, habits and social problems: *an insidious disease*, *insidious effects*, *the insidious spread of…*. It is always negative and stresses that the danger is hidden. Do not confuse it with *invidious*, which means unfair or likely to cause resentment.
entries.pattern: an insidious disease / threat / effect / influence; the insidious spread of something
examples: High blood pressure is **insidious**: most people feel nothing until something goes badly wrong.
Credit card debt grows in an **insidious** way, a few small purchases at a time.
Mold had been doing **insidious** damage behind the bathroom wall for years before we noticed.

drill.sentence: Loneliness is an {{insidious}} problem among older adults because it develops quietly over many years.
drill.hint: harmful in a slow way you don't notice (not *invisible* or *underlying*)

entries.related: *creeping* — slowly increasing, often before a noun; *pernicious* — very harmful, often in a gradual way, more formal; *invidious* — unfair or likely to cause resentment.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: No longer in contact with a family member or spouse because of a disagreement or a breakdown in the relationship.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation about family: *her estranged father*, *his estranged wife*, *estranged from his brother*. In news reports, *estranged wife* or *husband* often means separated but not yet divorced. Use *from* for the person: *She's been estranged from her mother for years*.
entries.pattern: someone's estranged father / wife / son; be estranged from someone
examples: She hadn't spoken to her **estranged** father in ten years when he called out of the blue.
The singer's **estranged** wife filed for divorce last month, according to court records.
He's been **estranged** from his brother since they fought over their mother's will.

drill.sentence: After years of silence, the two {{estranged}} sisters finally talked again at their cousin's wedding.
drill.hint: no longer in contact after a falling-out (not *feuding*)

entries.related: *alienated* — feeling isolated or cut off, more general; *separated* — married but living apart; *reconciled* — the opposite, back in contact.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: No longer relevant or worth discussing, because the situation has changed or the question has already been decided.
entries.usage: Most common in *a moot point* and after *be* or *become*: *The question became moot when…*. In American English it usually means *no longer relevant*, while in British English *a moot point* often means *open to debate*. American courts also call a case *moot* when there is no longer a real dispute to decide.
entries.pattern: a moot point; the question / issue is (now) moot; render something moot
examples: We argued about where to put the new couch, but it's a **moot** point: it doesn't fit through the door.
The lawsuit became **moot** after the city removed the sign.
Whether we should ask for a bigger budget is **moot** now that the project has been canceled.

drill.sentence: We spent an hour deciding which beach to go to, but the storm made the whole question {{moot}}.
drill.hint: no longer worth discussing (not *irrelevant* or *academic*)

mistake.why: The word is *moot* /mut/, rhyming with *boot*; *mute* /mjut/ means silent.

entries.related: *academic* — of no practical importance; *irrelevant* — not connected to the matter; *debatable* — still open to argument.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Power and influence over people, decisions or events, often because of money, position or popularity.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation about business, politics and celebrities: *political clout*, *financial clout*, *have the clout to…*. It sounds slightly informal and suggests real, practical power, not just status. In recent slang, *clout* also means online fame, as in *chasing clout*.
entries.pattern: political / financial / economic clout; have the clout to do something; use your clout
examples: Big retailers have the **clout** to demand lower prices from their suppliers.
Her uncle has a lot of **clout** in the restaurant world, so she got a table on short notice.
The players' union has much more **clout** than it did twenty years ago.

drill.sentence: The neighborhood association doesn't have much {{clout}} at city hall, so nobody listens when they complain about traffic.
drill.hint: practical power to get results (not *influence*, *power* or *pull*)

entries.related: *influence* — more neutral and general; *pull* — informal, influence through connections; *leverage* — power you can use in a negotiation.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not based on facts or evidence, and therefore not true or not justified.
entries.usage: Common in news, official statements and serious conversation with *fears*, *concerns*, *rumors* and *allegations*: *the fears proved unfounded*. It is a calm, neutral-sounding way to say something is wrong, so organizations use it to deny accusations politely. It is softer than *baseless* and is the usual word for worries that turn out to be unnecessary.
entries.pattern: unfounded fears / concerns / rumors / allegations; prove / turn out to be unfounded
examples: My worries about the new job turned out to be **unfounded**; my coworkers are great.
The company called the reports of layoffs completely **unfounded**.
Fears that the new bike lanes would hurt local shops have so far proved **unfounded**.

drill.sentence: Her fear that the dog would hate the new baby was {{unfounded}}: he follows the baby everywhere.
drill.hint: not supported by any real reason (not *misplaced*, *unjustified* or *unnecessary*)

entries.related: *baseless* — stronger, often for accusations; *groundless* — very close; *misplaced* — about feelings directed at the wrong thing; *well-founded* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not serious or sensible; spending time or money on things that have little value or purpose.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news, usually critical: *frivolous spending*, *a frivolous lawsuit*, *frivolous questions*. In American legal language, a *frivolous lawsuit* is one with no real legal basis. It can also be lighthearted and affectionate (*a frivolous pair of shoes*).
entries.pattern: frivolous spending / purchases / lawsuits / questions
examples: It may seem **frivolous**, but a good haircut really does make me feel more confident.
The judge dismissed the case as **frivolous** and ordered the plaintiff to pay the other side's legal fees.
We cut all **frivolous** spending this year to save for a down payment.

drill.sentence: My grandparents grew up poor, so they think spending six dollars on a latte is {{frivolous}}.
drill.hint: a silly waste on unimportant things (not *wasteful* or *extravagant*)

entries.related: *trivial* — unimportant; *flippant* — not showing proper seriousness, about remarks; *frugal* — careful with money, almost the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Rude and harsh in the way you talk or behave, so that people feel annoyed or hurt.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and workplace talk about personalities: *an abrasive manner*, *an abrasive personality*, *he can be abrasive*. It is a fairly strong criticism, so people often soften it with *a bit* or *can be*. Literally, *abrasive* describes rough materials that scrape, like sandpaper.
entries.pattern: an abrasive manner / personality / style; can be a bit abrasive
examples: Our new manager is brilliant but a bit **abrasive**, and a few people have already complained.
His **abrasive** comments at the town meeting didn't win him any friends.
The comedian's **abrasive** style isn't for everyone, but his fans love it.

drill.sentence: My uncle means well, but his {{abrasive}} way of giving advice makes everyone at dinner tense up.
drill.hint: rough and grating, like sandpaper (not *harsh*, *blunt* or *aggressive*)

entries.related: *brusque* — short and rude, often about speech; *blunt* — honest and direct, not always rude; *gracious* — the opposite, kind and polite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The point at which a plan, idea or hope finally becomes real, usually after a long time.
entries.usage: Used almost only in the fixed phrases *come to fruition* and *bring something to fruition*, in news, business and educated speech. It suggests years of work or waiting. It has three syllables with the stress on the second: froo-ISH-un.
entries.pattern: come to fruition; bring something to fruition
examples: The couple's plan to turn the old barn into a guesthouse finally came to **fruition** last summer.
She opened her own bakery at sixty, bringing a lifelong dream to **fruition**.
Few of the promises in the startup's pitch deck ever came to **fruition**.

drill.sentence: We talked about a family trip to Japan for years, and this spring it finally came to {{fruition}}.
drill.hint: became real after long planning (not *pass*)

entries.related: *come true* — about dreams and wishes, less formal; *materialize* — happen or appear, often in negatives; *come to pass* — literary, happen.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A clever, often slightly dishonest plan or action designed to gain an advantage over someone.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and conversation, usually with suspicion: *a marketing ploy*, *a clever ploy*, *a ploy to get attention*. It is lighter than *scheme* or *plot* and often suggests a trick that people can see through. Typical patterns are *a ploy to* + verb and *see through a ploy*.
entries.pattern: a ploy to + verb; a marketing / publicity / clever ploy; see through a ploy
examples: That "only two rooms left" message is just a **ploy** to make you book faster.
My son's sudden interest in helping with dinner was a **ploy** to stay up later.
Analysts dismissed the price cut as a publicity **ploy** ahead of the company's earnings report.

drill.sentence: The free cruise offer was just a {{ploy}} to get us into a three-hour sales pitch for a timeshare.
drill.hint: a clever move to gain an advantage (not *trick*, *ruse* or *gimmick*)

entries.related: *ruse* — a trick to deceive, more formal; *gimmick* — a trick to attract attention, often in marketing; *scheme* — a larger, more organized plan.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To have and use power, authority or influence, especially a large amount of it.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and analytical writing: *wield power*, *wield influence*, *wield enormous clout*. It suggests active, sometimes worrying use of power rather than simply having it. Literally, it means to hold and use a weapon or tool (*wielding a knife*).
entries.pattern: wield + power / influence / authority / a veto
examples: A handful of tech companies now **wield** enormous influence over what we see online.
In our family, Grandma **wields** the real power; even Dad checks with her before big decisions.
Referees **wield** a lot of authority, but one bad call can make them the most hated person in the stadium.

drill.sentence: As president of the homeowners' association, she {{wields}} more power than most people on the street realize.
drill.hint: actively uses (not *has*, *holds* or *exercises*)

entries.related: *exercise* — use a right or power, more neutral; *exert* — use influence or pressure; *hold* — simply have power.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A sudden, complete failure that is also embarrassing or humiliating.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and conversation, often with a hint of humor: *the whole thing was a debacle*, *the debacle over…*. It is used for launches, games, parties and public plans that go wrong in front of everyone. The stress is on the second syllable: dih-BAH-kul, sometimes dih-BAK-ul.
entries.pattern: a complete / total debacle; the debacle over / of something
examples: The product launch was a **debacle**: the website crashed and the demo failed on stage.
Our attempt to cook Thanksgiving dinner for twenty people turned into a total **debacle**.
After last season's embarrassing **debacle** in the playoffs, the coach was fired.

drill.sentence: The surprise party was a {{debacle}}: she walked in early, the cake hit the floor, and the dog ate it.
drill.hint: an embarrassing, complete failure (not *disaster* or *fiasco*)

entries.related: *fiasco* — very close, often slightly comic; *disaster* — more general; *flop* — informal, a failure with the public, like a movie.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To change and improve the form, look or structure of something, often to make it more modern or effective.
entries.usage: Common in business, news and design language: *revamp a website*, *revamp the menu*, *revamp a program*. It suggests a big change that still keeps the basic thing. It is also a noun: *the kitchen needs a revamp*.
entries.pattern: revamp + a website / menu / system / image; a complete revamp
examples: The diner **revamped** its menu, adding vegan options and dropping half the fried food.
The city plans to **revamp** the old train station, with a food hall downstairs and offices above.
We're **revamping** our onboarding process so new hires aren't lost in their first week.

drill.sentence: After twenty years, the airline finally {{revamped}} its frequent-flyer program, and most members aren't happy about it.
drill.hint: gave a major makeover to (not *overhauled*, *redesigned* or *reworked*)

entries.related: *overhaul* — examine and change completely, a bigger change; *update* — make current; *makeover* — informal noun, a change in appearance.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To give someone what they want, or make concessions, in order to calm them down or avoid conflict.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, history and serious conversation, and often critical: it suggests giving in too easily instead of solving the real problem. Typical objects are *critics*, *angry customers*, *investors* and *a crying child*. The noun *appeasement* is strongly linked to Britain's policy toward Hitler in the 1930s.
entries.pattern: appease + critics / customers / investors / a child; try to appease someone
examples: To **appease** angry passengers, the airline handed out meal vouchers after the five-hour delay.
Nothing I said could **appease** my toddler once his balloon popped.
The company replaced its CEO to **appease** investors, but the stock kept falling.

drill.sentence: The landlord offered us a month of free parking to {{appease}} us after the heat was out for a week.
drill.hint: calm us down by giving in a little (not *placate* or *pacify*)

entries.related: *placate* — calm someone who is angry, often temporarily; *pacify* — make calm, also used for babies; *stand up to* — the opposite, resist.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very loyal and firmly committed to a person, cause or belief over a long time.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, mainly before nouns: *a staunch ally*, *a staunch supporter*, *a staunch defender of*, *a staunch critic*. It suggests loyalty that does not change under pressure. The verb *staunch* (or *stanch*), as in *staunch the bleeding*, means to stop a flow.
entries.pattern: a staunch ally / supporter / defender / critic (of something)
examples: My grandfather was a **staunch** Yankees fan until the day he died.
The two countries have been **staunch** allies since the end of World War II.
She's a **staunch** defender of public libraries and speaks at every budget meeting.

drill.sentence: Even after the restaurant got bad reviews, my cousin remained its {{staunchest}} supporter and ate there every Friday.
drill.hint: most firmly loyal and committed (not *biggest* or *strongest*)

entries.related: *steadfast* — firm and unchanging, more literary; *loyal* — the everyday word; *ardent* — enthusiastic and passionate; *lukewarm* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The way a person looks and behaves, which shows their mood or character to others.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, legal reports and descriptions of people: *a calm demeanor*, *his cheerful demeanor*, *her professional demeanor*. It describes the outward impression, often in contrast with what someone feels inside. The British spelling is *demeanour*.
entries.pattern: a calm / friendly / cheerful / professional demeanor
examples: Despite her calm **demeanor**, the pilot later admitted she'd been terrified during the landing.
The witness's nervous **demeanor** made the jury doubt his story.
Our vet has such a gentle **demeanor** that even our anxious cat relaxes around her.

drill.sentence: Behind his cheerful {{demeanor}}, my brother was struggling more than any of us knew.
drill.hint: the way he appeared and behaved to others (not *exterior*, *facade* or *manner*)

entries.related: *manner* — the way someone behaves toward others; *bearing* — the way someone stands and moves, more formal; *facade* — a false outward appearance.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make something, usually something bad such as a myth or an unfair situation, continue for a long time.
entries.usage: Common in academic, journalistic and social writing: *perpetuate a myth*, *perpetuate stereotypes*, *perpetuate a cycle of poverty*. It is almost always critical. The subject is often a habit, a system or the media, rather than a single person.
entries.pattern: perpetuate + a myth / stereotype / cycle / problem
examples: Cartoons that show stepmothers as evil **perpetuate** an unfair stereotype.
The idea that we use only ten percent of our brains is a myth that movies keep **perpetuating**.
Payday loans can **perpetuate** a cycle of debt that's very hard to escape.

drill.sentence: Every time we pay the kids to do their homework, we {{perpetuate}} the idea that learning is a chore.
drill.hint: keep alive for a long time (not *reinforce*, *promote* or *feed*)

mistake.wrong: The robbery was perpetuated by two teenagers.
mistake.right: The robbery was perpetrated by two teenagers.
mistake.why: *Perpetrate* means commit a crime or harmful act; *perpetuate* means make something continue.

entries.related: *maintain* — keep something at the same level, neutral; *reinforce* — make stronger; *perpetrate* — commit a crime, a different word.
